reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: The classic triad is postprandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina), fear of eating (sitophobia) and weight loss.

Almost always caused by atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusion of two or more of the three mesenteric vessels (coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries) because of rich collateralisation.
Predominantly affects older women who smoke and have widespread atherosclerosis.
Pain characteristically begins within about 15 to 30 minutes of eating and is disproportionate to examination findings.
Weight loss stems from reduced intake because of food fear rather than malabsorption, and can closely mimic malignancy.
Duplex ultrasound is a useful screening test; CT angiography confirms the diagnosis and plans revascularisation.
Endovascular angioplasty and stenting is now first-line revascularisation for most patients, with open bypass or endarterectomy reserved for complex disease or endovascular failure.
Untreated disease can progress to acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia and bowel infarction.
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive atherosclerotic narrowing of the ostia of the coeliac axis and superior mesenteric artery reduces splanchnic blood flow. Because of the extensive collateral network, including the pancreaticoduodenal arcades and the marginal artery of Drummond with the arc of Riolan, symptoms usually develop only when at least two of the three main vessels are critically diseased. After eating, splanchnic oxygen demand rises but the stenotic vessels cannot augment flow, producing a supply-demand mismatch and ischaemic visceral pain, with blood effectively diverted from the intestinal to the gastric circulation. Chronic ischaemia impairs mucosal integrity, and acute thrombosis of a critical vessel precipitates transmural infarction. Non-atherosclerotic causes include median arcuate ligament compression, vasculitis and fibromuscular dysplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Intra-abdominal malignancy such as gastric or pancreatic cancer causing weight loss
additionalInvestigations: Mesenteric duplex ultrasound with fasting and postprandial velocities
CT angiography of the mesenteric vessels
Catheter angiography with a lateral aortogram, often with intervention
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and cross-sectional imaging to exclude malignancy or ulceration
Nutritional assessment and baseline blood tests
Screening for vasculitis where the presentation is atypical
redFlags: Sudden severe constant abdominal pain, or pain out of proportion, signalling acute-on-chronic ischaemia or infarction.
Peritonism, lactic acidosis or a rising white cell count.
Rapid, profound weight loss and malnutrition.
reference.prognosis: Successful revascularisation relieves symptoms, restores weight and prevents progression to infarction in the great majority, whereas untreated disease risks acute mesenteric infarction with very high mortality. Endovascular treatment carries lower perioperative morbidity but higher restenosis than open repair, mandating surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing weight loss and pain to occult malignancy and pursuing an exhaustive negative work-up while missing the vascular cause.
Assuming single-vessel stenosis explains symptoms when disease of at least two vessels or specific superior mesenteric artery involvement is usually required.
Delaying revascularisation until acute infarction supervenes.
Overlooking median arcuate ligament compression in younger patients.
Providing inadequate surveillance after stenting and missing restenosis.
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
European Society for Vascular Surgery clinical practice guidelines on the management of mesenteric ischaemia
management: Revascularisation as definitive treatment by endovascular angioplasty and stenting, or by surgical bypass or endarterectomy, to relieve intestinal angina and prevent infarction
Cardiovascular risk-factor modification with smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy and statin treatment
Nutritional support and repletion for weight loss and malnutrition before and after intervention
Emergency surgical management of the acute-on-chronic presentation with bowel infarction
Exclusion of malignancy and other causes of weight loss through endoscopy and cross-sectional imaging
Duplex surveillance of stent and graft patency given the restenosis risk after endovascular treatment, under vascular surgery care
